headline: Tradition carries wisdom across generations—but traditions must be understood, not just followed blindly
universal_truth: What persists often has hidden value; but what persists can also be outdated—wisdom is knowing which is which
fun_facts: Many traditions that seem arbitrary originally solved practical problems—their reasons got lost while the practice continued
Breaking tradition too quickly can destroy accumulated wisdom; keeping it too long can trap you in obsolete patterns
Every tradition was once an innovation that worked well enough to be repeated
discussion_questions: Which traditions in your life are meaningful versus automatic?
How do you decide which traditions to keep and which to abandon?
What new traditions have you created?

hook.script: Why do we shake hands? Celebrate birthdays? Work Monday through Friday? Many practices continue simply because they always have. But traditions aren't random—most started for reasons. Those reasons might be lost, obsolete, or still valid.

cliff.script: Some traditions seem pointless, but contain hidden wisdom. Others really are obsolete. How do you tell the difference between valuable tradition and outdated habit?

options.text: Ask what problem the tradition originally solved, whether that problem still exists, and whether the tradition still solves it effectively
options.response: Yes. Traditions are solutions to problems. If the problem persists and the solution works, keep it. If the problem has changed or better solutions exist, the tradition can evolve.

options.text: Traditions that have lasted a long time are probably valuable
options.response: Longevity suggests value, but context changes—old solutions can become obsolete...

fact1.title: Encoded Wisdom
fact1.script: Traditions often encode solutions to problems we've forgotten. Food taboos sometimes prevented disease. Social rituals sometimes maintained peace. The practice survived even when the reason was lost. Respect tradition before rejecting it.

fact2.title: Chesterton's Fence
fact2.script: G.K. Chesterton said: don't remove a fence until you know why it was put up. Traditions are fences—before you tear them down, understand their purpose. They might be protecting something you can't see.

fact3.title: Conscious Tradition
fact3.script: The best approach: understand traditions, then consciously choose which to keep, modify, or abandon. Blind following is dangerous. Blind rejection is arrogant. Understanding enables wise choice.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: What persists often has hidden value. But what persists can also be outdated. Wisdom is knowing which is which—and that requires understanding.

outro.script: That's Day 209. Tomorrow, we'll explore better ways of doing things—progress. Until then, pick a tradition you follow and try to discover why it started.

growTrack.title: Tradition Archaeology - Why This Practice?
growTrack.activity: Pick one tradition you follow—personal, family, or cultural. Research or think about why it started. What problem did it solve? Does that problem still exist? Is the solution still effective? This conscious engagement improves your relationship with tradition.
